summary: Isoxsuprine is a beta-adrenergic agonist with direct smooth muscle relaxant activity, historically used as a peripheral vasodilator for peripheral vascular disorders and as a uterine relaxant (tocolytic) to manage threatened preterm labour in some countries. Efficacy in peripheral vascular disease is poorly substantiated and the drug has been withdrawn in many markets and is not currently FDA-approved. This record is pending clinical review.
indications: Symptomatic relief of peripheral vascular disorders such as Raynaud's phenomenon, intermittent claudication, and other conditions associated with peripheral vasospasm or arterial insufficiency (efficacy not well established)
Uterine relaxant (tocolytic) for threatened or established preterm labour in countries where licensed

moa: Isoxsuprine stimulates beta-adrenergic receptors and also exerts a direct relaxant effect on vascular and uterine smooth muscle. Beta-2 receptor stimulation relaxes arterial smooth muscle, producing peripheral vasodilation and increasing skeletal muscle blood flow, and relaxes the myometrium to inhibit uterine contractions. It may also have mild beta-1 effects causing increases in heart rate and cardiac output, and can lower blood pressure through vasodilation.

preg: Pending clinical review - not FDA-approved. Used in some countries as a tocolytic (uterine relaxant) for preterm labour, but only under specialist obstetric supervision with maternal and fetal monitoring. It is contraindicated where there is haemorrhage in pregnancy and in the immediate postpartum period. Do not use outside a licensed tocolytic indication.
lact: Safety during breastfeeding has not been established; use is not recommended. If used, observe the infant for signs of beta-adrenergic effects such as tachycardia.
renal: Limited data in renal impairment; use with caution and monitor for cardiovascular effects.
hepatic: Limited data in hepatic impairment; use with caution.

pearls: Pending clinical review - not FDA-approved; withdrawn in several markets and efficacy in peripheral vascular disease is poorly substantiated
Acts as a beta-adrenergic agonist and direct smooth muscle relaxant on both vasculature and myometrium
Tocolytic (uterine relaxant) use is restricted to specialist obstetric settings with maternal and fetal monitoring
Contraindicated in arterial bleeding, antepartum haemorrhage, and the immediate postpartum period
Watch for tachycardia, palpitations, hypotension, and (with parenteral beta-agonist use) pulmonary oedema
Avoid in significant ischaemic heart disease, tachyarrhythmias, and recent myocardial infarction
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose and resume the normal schedule. Do not double up.
overdose: Overdose may cause exaggerated beta-adrenergic and vasodilator effects including marked hypotension, tachycardia, palpitations, flushing, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with positioning, intravenous fluids for hypotension, and cardiac monitoring. A cautious beta-blocker may be considered for severe tachyarrhythmia under specialist guidance.
